findings.claim: The Piracy Act (1717) created vice-admiralty courts in the colonies so pirates could be tried locally (repeated in the key fact, the match set, a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Colonial piracy trials were authorised by the Piracy Act 1698 (royal assent 1700), continued in 1706 and made perpetual in 1719. The 1717 Act (4 Geo. 1 c. 11) was the Transportation Act; its section 7 dealt with penalties for piracy, including death. The spec names the Act but does not say what it did.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Piracy Act 1698' (An Act for the more effectual Suppression of Piracy; trials 'in any of his Majesty's islands, plantations, colonies'); Wikipedia 'Piracy Act 1717' / 'Transportation Act 1717'.

findings.claim: By 1740, around 150,000 enslaved Africans worked the Chesapeake.
findings.truth: About 150,000 was the enslaved population of all thirteen colonies in 1740 (16.6 per cent of roughly 905,000). Virginia and Maryland together held roughly 85,000. The lesson's 1770 figure (over 250,000 in the Chesapeake) is right.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Historical racial and ethnic demographics of the United States' (1740 Black share 16.6% of the thirteen colonies); Wikipedia 'Colony of Virginia' (total Virginia population 180,440 in 1740).

findings.claim: The Negro Act of 1740 banned enslaved people from 'learning to read or write' (repeated in a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Act banned teaching enslaved people to write. Reading was not prohibited.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Negro Act of 1740': prohibited from 'learn to write (though reading was not proscribed)'.

findings.claim: Stono contributed to the build-up of friction that became the War of Jenkins' Ear later that year.
findings.truth: Cause and effect are reversed. The war's causes (Spanish coastguards, the Jenkins hearings of 1738) long predate the rising, and Britain declared war on Spain in October 1739, six weeks after Stono. Historians argue the reverse link: news of an approaching war probably influenced the rebels' timing.
findings.evidence: Chronology: Stono 9 September 1739; British declaration of war on Spain 23 October 1739.

findings.claim: Around 150 people were arrested, including 20 white New Yorkers (1741).
findings.truth: 161 Black New Yorkers and 20 white New Yorkers were arrested - about 180 in all.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'New York Conspiracy of 1741': 'By the end of the trials, 161 blacks and 20 whites had been arrested.'

findings.claim: 'For a 4-mark Describe Two Features question...'
findings.truth: Describe two features is the British depth study form. The period study paper sets a consequence task, an analytical narrative and two importance parts only.
findings.evidence: Edexcel 1HI0 spec, Paper 2 assessment information: booklet P questions 1(a)/1(b) consequence, 2 analytical narrative, 3 importance (two parts from three).

findings.claim: 'For a 4-mark Describe Two Features question...'
findings.truth: Same as F6: this form belongs to the British depth study, not the period study.
findings.evidence: Edexcel 1HI0 spec, Paper 2 assessment information.

findings.claim: Newspapers grew to 'over forty by the 1760s' - repeated in the key fact, the conclusion, a mark scheme, a flashcard, and a knowledge check whose marked answer is 'forty'.
findings.truth: There were 24 weekly newspapers in the thirteen colonies by the mid-1760s; the number reached about 37 only by 1775.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'History of American newspapers': 'By the mid-1760s, there were 24 weekly newspapers in the 13 colonies.'

findings.claim: Whitefield 'toured the colonies seven times from 1739 onwards' (repeated in a knowledge check stem).
findings.truth: Whitefield made seven voyages to America; the first was in 1738 to Georgia. The famous revival tour began in 1739.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'George Whitefield': seven voyages, the first in 1738.

findings.claim: Washington 'clashed with French troops at the Forks of the Ohio' in 1754.
findings.truth: The French already held the Forks (Fort Duquesne). Washington's skirmish was at Jumonville Glen, south-east of the Forks, on 28 May 1754; Fort Necessity followed in July.
findings.evidence: Standard chronology of the Jumonville Glen skirmish and Fort Duquesne.

findings.claim: The smallpox blankets at Fort Pitt were 'an act ordered by Amherst himself' (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: The Fort Pitt garrison (William Trent and Captain Simeon Ecuyer) gave Delaware negotiators two blankets and a handkerchief from the smallpox hospital on 24 June 1763, independently. Amherst wrote to Bouquet on 8 July 1763 asking whether smallpox could be sent among the nations in revolt - two weeks after the event.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Siege of Fort Pitt': Trent's journal, 24 June 1763; Amherst to Bouquet, 8 July 1763; the plan was 'carried out independently from General Amherst and Colonel Bouquet'.

findings.claim: James Otis 'published a pamphlet objecting that taxation without representation is tyranny' (repeated in a flashcard and a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The phrase does not appear in Otis's writings. It was in use in Boston by 1765 and first appeared in print in a London Magazine headline in February 1768. His 1764 pamphlet argued that Parliament could not tax colonists who sent no members to it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'No taxation without representation'.

findings.claim: The Paxton Boys came 'from Lancaster County in western Pennsylvania' (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: Lancaster County is in south-eastern Pennsylvania. Paxton, near modern Harrisburg, was then the colony's frontier, but not the west.
findings.evidence: Geography of Lancaster County and Paxton township.

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward students who can show contingency' and 'Examiners cap that response in the middle bands' in the lesson body.
findings.truth: Invented claims about examiner behaviour. The house vocabulary describes the band, not the examiner.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: invented exam claims are removed.

findings.claim: On 19 April 1775, 73 British soldiers were dead 'and around 95 were wounded'.
findings.truth: British losses were 73 killed, 174 wounded and 53 missing.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battles of Lexington and Concord'.

findings.claim: 'The third force was beaten back at Oriskany.'
findings.truth: St Leger's force from Lake Ontario abandoned its siege of Fort Stanwix in August 1777 after its Indigenous allies withdrew. Oriskany, 6 August 1777, was an ambush of the American relief militia, not the defeat of St Leger's column.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Saratoga campaign': 'St. Leger was forced to abandon the siege.'

findings.claim: After North fell in March 1782, 'Britain's new ministry under Lord Shelburne sought a settlement' (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: Rockingham succeeded North in March 1782; Shelburne took over only in July 1782, after Rockingham's death.
findings.evidence: Ministerial dates, 1782.

findings.claim: 'From 1779 the British shifted strategy southwards... They captured Savannah and Charleston.'
findings.truth: Savannah fell in December 1778, so the southern strategy begins in late 1778.
findings.evidence: Capture of Savannah, 29 December 1778.

findings.claim: 'Cherokee, Creek and Shawnee fought British alliances.'
findings.truth: They fought on the British side. As written the sentence says the opposite.
findings.evidence: Spec key topic 3 and standard accounts of Indigenous alignment in the war.

findings.claim: 'the Niagara region' is defined as the region around the Niagara River 'where the British Crown granted around 950,000 acres' to the Iroquois.
findings.truth: The Haldimand Tract of about 950,000 acres runs along the Grand River in what is now southern Ontario, not around the Niagara River. The spec uses 'Niagara' for the Loyalist resettlement area.
findings.evidence: Haldimand Proclamation 1784, Grand River tract.

findings.claim: The 1792 Freetown settlement was 'the first organised return to Africa by people of African descent in the Atlantic world' (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: An earlier organised settlement, Granville Town, was founded in 1787 by about 400 formerly enslaved people sent from London; Freetown was built on its site in 1792.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Freetown'.

findings.claim: All 25 'Explain two consequences of...' practice questions across the unit are labelled '4 marks - Consequence Question'.
findings.truth: On this paper the two-consequence task is worth 8 marks, 4 for each consequence (4 + 4 + 8 narrative + 16 importance = 32). A 4-mark label on a two-consequence stem tells students to write half the required answer. The alternative reading - that the label means 4 marks per consequence - is not what the student sees on the card, and the mark schemes already describe a full two-consequence answer.
findings.evidence: Edexcel 1HI0 spec, Paper 2: booklet P is 32 marks, questions 1(a) and 1(b) on consequence, question 2 analytical narrative, question 3 two importance parts.

findings.claim: 'examiners reward...' appears in the exam tips of lessons 1, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12.
findings.truth: Invented claims about examiner behaviour; replaced with house band vocabulary.
findings.evidence: Checker brief.

findings.claim: 'By 1750, Philadelphia was the largest city in British America' (repeated in a flashcard).
findings.truth: Boston was still marginally the larger town in 1750; Philadelphia passed it during the 1750s and was clearly the largest by 1760. No approved source could be reached to fix the date, so the claim is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Could not verify from Wikipedia in this session.

findings.claim: 'The Edexcel specification, updated for first assessment in 2026, uses enslaved person rather than slave.'
findings.truth: The terminology point is right, but the qualification's first assessment was 2018. Issue 6, June 2024, made minor amends to P2 content that take effect for assessment from summer 2026.
findings.evidence: Edexcel 1HI0 spec, summary of Issue 6 changes: 'These changes will take effect for assessment from summer 2026.'

findings.claim: 'the merchant Samuel Adams'.
findings.truth: Adams inherited a malt house but is better described as Boston's tax collector and the movement's political organiser; the merchants of the Loyal Nine were other men.
findings.evidence: Standard biographies.

findings.claim: 'the French alliance it produced added 12,000 troops at Yorktown'.
findings.truth: French land forces at Yorktown numbered about 10,800, alongside 8,000-9,000 Americans.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Siege of Yorktown': French '10,800 men and 29 warships'.

findings.claim: 'the Royal African Company opened up greater supply' of enslaved people.
findings.truth: The company held a monopoly that limited supply. The Trade with Africa Act 1697 opened the trade to independent merchants on a ten per cent levy, after which the numbers exported doubled.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Royal African Company': monopoly lost in 1697; 'the price of enslaved Africans and the number exported doubled'.

summary: All 12 lessons checked against the Edexcel 1HI0 P2 content bullets and the Paper 2 assessment information. Twenty-eight findings: five HIGH (the Piracy Act 1717 credited with creating colonial vice-admiralty courts; two exam tips setting the British-depth describe-two-features question; a colonial newspaper count that a knowledge check marks correct; the Fort Pitt smallpox blankets attributed to an order from Amherst), fifteen MEDIUM and eight LOW. Seventy-eight edits, including the unit-wide relabelling of the 25 two-consequence questions from 4 marks to 8.
